newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA WHEAT GOOD DESPITE BAD WEATHER - OFFICIAL.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA WHEAT GOOD DESPITE BAD WEATHER - OFFICIAL.

text.p: Romania's 1997 wheat crop will have a good quality despite the adverse weather in recent days and this year's exports will not be affected, a senior Romanian official said on Monday.

"There is no reason to believe that the quality of the wheat crop has diminished following last week's meteorological conditions," Trita Fanita, chairman of the Senate's Commission for agriculture, woods and food industry, said in a statement.

The statement was in response to remarks made last week by Vasile Duta, the head of the National Agency for Agricultural Products, who said rains over the past week had affected the quality of Romania's milling wheat and consequently exports could be lower than the planned 2.4 million tonnes.
The Agriculture Ministry expects a bumper wheat crop of 7.07 million tonnes in 1997, almost double the level last year.
Romania and other Eastern European countries including Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Yugoslavia, was not spared by bad weather last week.
But Fanita, who is also the general manager of the local Agroexport SA, a major grain trading company, said the adverse weather had no impact on Romania's wheat crop.
"This year, the good wheat crop has a quality which makes it fit for milling. Consequently it will be asked for export," Fanita said.
On Monday, an expert at the Institute for agricultural research in Fundulea, near Bucharest, said that only part of the wheat harvested so far had been hit by bad weather.
"I wouldn't say that the majority of the wheat crop has been affected, from the quality point of view," he added.
He said wheat harvested in the western counties of Banat and Oradea showed "the beginning of a germination process in the (wheat's) ear."
"This affects to a certain extent the quality of the wheat harvested in that area," the expert said.
The Fundulea institute had not received similar reports on the condition of the wheat harvested in the southern regions, traditionally the country's main grain suppliers, he said.
"It is true that it rained there every day, but luckily it was for short periods of time, and such (germination) process has not started," the expert said.
